newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Exiled activist urges China to release dissidents.
newsitem.headline: Exiled activist urges China to release dissidents.

text.p: A Chinese labour activist in exile in Hong Kong has demanded China immediately halt its repression of the independent labour movement and release all detained labour and democracy activists.

Han Dongfang, in a statement received by Reuters on Friday, urged Beijing to allow Chinese workers the right to unionise and to grant detained political and labour activists statutory rights, including access to basic medical care and prison visits.

"Yet again, we strongly condemn the persecution of independent trade union activists by the Chinese government as well as the original judgement passed on Liu Nianchun by the Beijing Chaoyang District People's Court," he said in the statement dated Thursday.
"The decision was totally unfair and constituted a political judgement in accordance with the wishes of the government."

Last month, a Chinese court rejected Liu's appeal against a labour camp term for writing a petition urging Beijing to re-evaluate its crackdown on student demonstrators in Tiananmen Square on June 4, 1989, and to free all political prisoners.
Last July, police ordered Liu, a 48-year-old veteran dissident, to serve three years of re-education through labour on top of nearly a year in detention for drafting the petition.
He was also accused of accepting illegal aid from abroad and of trying to form a group to promote protection of workers' rights.
Re-education through labour is a form of administrative punishment that can be imposed by authorities without recourse to prosecutors or the courts.
On Thursday, Washington accused China of effectively silencing all public dissent against the communist party and government in 1996.

"The Chinese government in 1996 continued to commit widespread and well-documented human rights abuses, in violation of internationally accepted norms, stemming from the authorities' intolerance of dissent, fear of unrest and the continuing absence of laws protecting basic freedoms," the U.S. State Department said in its annual human rights report.
China on Tuesday praised its human rights record and said there were no political prisoners in the country.

"So-called political prisoners do not exist in China," Foreign Ministry spokesman Shen Guofang told reporters. "...The Chinese government has made efforts...to promote and protect human rights and basic freedoms."
Han called on Beijing to accept that free speech and organisation of trade unions were not crimes.
Han was jailed for his role in the 1989 democracy movement and released after two years for medical treatment in the United States.
When he tried to return to China in 1993, his passport was cancelled, forcing him into exile in Hong Kong, which in July returns to Chinese rule after more than 150 years of British rule.
